Engineer here...

Yes the cable can be a bottleneck. The phone measures it's charge rate based on voltage drop over the cable. As you draw more current, the voltage drop increases.

Using a thicker gauge wire will reduce the voltage drop across the lines, thus allowing for more power to be drawn.

This is why fast charging uses a higher voltage rather than more current. Less losses in the system. In the end the higher voltage is only for delivery, as it is reduced to the battery voltage before reaching the battery. This lowers the voltage but increases amperage, allowing more power to be delivered over the same lines as normal charging.

You are correct in the fact that the cable can be a bottleneck. See comment below.

However, current is drawn, or pulled, not pushed. A 100 amp charger will still only deliver 2 amps to your device (assuming the device pulls 2 amps. )

When you use a charger with a lower current limit than your phone's attempted current draw you can damage the charger, or it will keep folding back on itself and charge intermittently.

You are right, I tested this. I bought a few cheap ass chinese cable and some high quality. Also wit hdifferent lengths, so I could for once and forever silence people who talk about long cables being worse.

Conclusion: It is the usb plug that matters. All the cables had like a few ohm/m, it was all in the connector plugs.

So if you want a long great working cable, buy yourself a 5 euro 30cm usb cable and some wire (or a 2m chinese one for 1 dollar) and slder the connectors on that 2m cable.

Yes. I was very annoyed when my gf bought an iphone 7 and it came with the same 1 amp charger as all the ones before. iPad chargers are 2.4 I believe. As far as charging faster, they probably deliver a more precise voltage which ensures the correct current. v=ir and all that, if a charger is even .1 volts low and the cable used is even a little bit crappy and has a very slightly higher than expected resistance it can reduce the charge current by almost half. The output ratings are the max the device will deliver under ideal conditions with no resistance in the circuit.

If you want to slow your charge rate it has to be done at the device requesting the amperage. Otherwise it will still try to draw the same current, but overtax your charger.

The slow and fast chargers for usb 2 had an added resistor that told your phone it was ok to draw more power, thus the phone requests more power, which the charger can deliver.

If it wasn't for this, when you plugged your phone into a regular usb port it would try to draw 2 amps through the port, which will cause problems.

The cord doesn't matter, they're all certified up to 60 watts if I remember correctly, all the real ones at least. Type C can dynamically charge devices at their maximum charging capacity. So I can use the 60W charger from my Chromebook Pixel laptop to safely charge my Nexus 5X at 15W or a Pixel C tablet at 25. I'm using Google products as examples because Google had a really large part in making Type C, so their ecosystem is kinda the hallmark here. It's worth mentioning that tons of Type C chargers and wires aren't up to snuff. My aunt bought a car charger for her Type C phone and the Type C connector fused itself to the phone because it's amperage was too high for the phone.

In other words, it's the charger. If you get a Type A to Type C wire and a cheap 5 watt 1.0 amp Type A power brick, you'll charge at 5W 1A.

Now, what device were you trying to charge, and why did you want to charge it slowly? If you charge something with an insufficient charger, you can risk damaging both devices, though damage to the charger is more likely.
